title: Faithfulness
hook: keep promises to your spouse and your people

segments.voice: Yesterday, do not kill, traced back to contempt in the heart. Your line was not even in the heart. Which word did you catch before it got out? Day one thousand one hundred ninety.

On the road out of Moab, three widows stop walking. Naomi, the mother-in-law, tells her two daughters-in-law to go home. She has nothing left to give them. One, Orpah, kisses her goodbye and turns back. The other, Ruth, won't let go: "whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." Those words aren't spoken between a husband and wife. They're spoken between two women with nothing left but each other. Today: faithfulness, the commandment about adultery, and the larger thing it protects.

The commandment itself is short: "Thou shalt not commit adultery." It guards marriage, the promise two people make to belong to each other. But scripture keeps setting that promise inside a bigger one: God's faithfulness to people who aren't always faithful back. The prophet Hosea is told to keep loving a wife who leaves him, as a living picture of God's love for a wandering people. Lamentations, a book of grief over a ruined city, still says: "great is thy faithfulness." And the second letter to Timothy says: "If we believe not, yet he abideth faithful: he cannot deny himself." In this reading, faithfulness isn't first a rule about bodies. It's a reflection of who God is. Jesus takes this commandment inward, the way he did with killing: he says that looking at someone with lust is already adultery in the heart. The point is that faithfulness starts where nobody else can see. And the commandment's reach goes wider than marriage. Ruth isn't married to Naomi. She simply won't leave. Friendships, families, congregations and teams all run on kept promises. Churches differ on marriage and divorce. Catholics and Orthodox Christians understand marriage as a sacrament; the Catholic Church teaches that a valid sacramental marriage, once consummated, can't be dissolved, while Orthodox churches can allow a second marriage in some cases. Protestant churches hold a range of views. Underneath all of them, the commandment asks the same plain thing: when you've given your word, keep it.

Here's the practice: keep one promise fully. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a promise you're keeping halfway. I'll call more. I'll be there. I'll fix that. I'll stop. It might be to a spouse, a friend, a child, a team. Hold it honestly, without excuses and without beating yourself up. What would keeping it fully look like this week? Find one concrete act. If you pray, you can ask God for help to keep it. The bell holds the time.
Faithfulness. Keeping the promises you've made, to a spouse and to your people, the way scripture says God keeps his.

Your line: faithful. Today, do the concrete act for that promise. And that's a week of commandments: no other gods, no idols, the Name, the sabbath, parents, killing, and now faithfulness. Day one thousand one hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Christians make vows of faithfulness at weddings, and Ruth's words to Naomi are sometimes read at them; churches teach this commandment as faithfulness in marriage, though Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches differ on divorce and remarriage.

notes: 'Written among ruins' for Lamentations rests on the book's content (laments over Jerusalem's fall); no date given. Confirm.
2 Timothy is attributed to Paul ('Paul writes'), following the letter's own opening; some scholars dispute authorship. Keeper may prefer 'the second letter to Timothy says'.
Hosea paraphrased (Hosea 1–3) as 'told to keep loving a wife who leaves him'; confirm.
Church teaching on marriage: Catholic (valid sacramental marriage indissoluble), Orthodox (can allow a second marriage in some cases), Protestant (a range). Confirm each is fair and unranked.
howItsDone says Ruth 1:16 is 'sometimes read' at weddings; confirm or cut.

Editor pass: hook's 'the oldest, Naomi' (an age claim the text doesn't make) became 'Naomi, the mother-in-law'; 'Lamentations, written among ruins' (a composition claim) became 'a book of grief over a ruined city', which rests on the book's content.

Audit pass (2026-10-02): 'Paul writes' (2 Timothy, authorship disputed) changed to 'the second letter to Timothy says' in teach and myth. Catholic teaching sharpened: it is a valid sacramental marriage, once consummated, that the Church holds cannot be dissolved (natural marriages can be, by the Pauline privilege), so 'a valid marriage' was imprecise.
